cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: The criminal justice system involves: police (investigate), CPS (prosecute), courts (try), sentencing (punish), probation (supervise in community), prison (custodial sentences).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: The police are responsible for preventing and detecting crime, maintaining public order, and protecting life and property. Police officers have powers of arrest, stop and search, and detention.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) reviews evidence gathered by the police and decides whether to charge — applying the Full Code Test (sufficient evidence + public interest).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Trial by jury is available for serious criminal offences ('indictable offences') in the Crown Court. The jury of 12 citizens decides the verdict; the judge decides the sentence.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Sentencing aims: retribution (punishment), deterrence (discouraging reoffending and others), rehabilitation (reforming the offender), and protection of the public.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Prison serves to protect the public and punish serious offenders, but the UK has one of the highest prison populations in Western Europe and reoffending rates are around 46% within one year.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Community orders require offenders to complete requirements in the community: unpaid work, curfew, rehabilitation programmes, or drug treatment. They are cheaper and can be more effective than short prison sentences.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Restorative justice brings offenders and victims together to address the harm caused. It can give victims closure and reduce reoffending, but is not appropriate for all cases.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Youth courts handle cases involving 10-17 year olds. They are less formal than adult courts: no public gallery, no wigs, parents must attend, and reporting restrictions apply.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: The probation service supervises offenders serving community sentences and those released from prison on licence, monitoring compliance and providing rehabilitation support.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Victims have rights under the Victims' Code including being informed about their case, making a Victim Personal Statement, and being told about an offender's release.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Justice System
cards.back: Anti-social behaviour powers include Community Protection Notices, Criminal Behaviour Orders, and dispersal powers, replacing the previous ASBO regime.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — the justice system?
cards.back: 1. For The Justice System questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link The Justice System to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate the effectiveness of the UK justice system in achieving fairness. [12 marks]

AO1 (Knowledge & Understanding — 30%): You need to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the justice system, including key concepts, legal frameworks, and institutional structures. AO2 (Analysis & Evaluation — 40%): You must analyse and evaluate different viewpoints, policies, and approaches related to the justice system.
